newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: China takes new step to accelerate WTO accession.
newsitem.headline: China takes new step to accelerate WTO accession.

text.p: In a move designed to speed up its membership in the World Trade Organisation (WTO), China pledged not to make any new laws or trade policies inconsistent with the WTO, assistant trade minister Long Yongtu said on Friday.

The commitment, made during a meeting of the WTO working party negotiating the terms of Beijing's entry into the 125-member watchdog, was welcomed by major trading nations including the United States, European Union, Japan and Canada, according to trade officials.
Long, speaking to reporters, said he sensed a "much more pragmatic and positive" approach by the U.S. delegation, led by Deborah Lehr, assistant secretary U.S. Trade Representative.
"They have taken away some purely bilateral trade issues outside the WTO framework," he said, referring to the U.S. "We agreed not to put all our laundry into one basket."
"We think things are on the right track," Long added, declining to predict when China might gain entry into the club.
Pierre-Louis Girard, a Swiss who chairs the WTO working party studying China's nine-year old application, announced that he would look into holding the next formal talks in February.

"In order to ensure future negotiations are carried out on a stable basis and to demonstrate China's sincerity to accelerate the negotiation, we hereby announce the decision of the Chinese government to undertake the principle of standstill, and commit ourselves that China will not promulgate new laws and policies inconsistent with the WTO rules during the negotiation process," Long said in a speech to the closed-door meeting.
"And in that spirit, we sincerely hope that the WTO members will not raise the threshold and increase trade restrictions against China in the meantime," he added.
"We believe that there is now a better opportunity for us to finally reach a package of agreements on the (accession) protocol and market acess through substantive negotiations."
The so-called "standstill" commitment is standard for countries in an advanced stage of negotiations, giving their trading partners a benchmark by which to measure them.
China's commitment was welcomed by countries including the United States, European Union, Japan, Canada, South Korea, Singapore, New Zealand, Norway and Cuba, trade officials said.
"This announcement of course was welcomed by major trading nations, by everybody in the room," said one official.
Lehr of the U.S. delegation welcomed the standstill commitment as a sign of China's serious intent to begin negotiations, calling it a foundation on which to move ahead, according to trade officials.
U.S. delegates held bilateral talks with the Chinese team in Geneva on Monday and Tuesday.
The EU's Roderick Abbott said the Chinese pledge was very positive and announced his delegation would hold bilateral talks with the Chinese delegation on Tuesday.
He called for all WTO members and Beijing to be flexible and innovative so as to find a solution.
